## skipgram {#skipgram}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## n-gram model
In the fields of computational linguistics, an **n-gram** is a contiguous sequence of n words (or other items) from a given sample of text or speech.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
plot_skipgram()
plt.plot()
```

- The skip-gram model assumes that a word can be used to generate its surrounding words in a text sequence. 
- Here, “the”, “man”, “loves”, “his”, "dog" is a text window of five words and the center word is "loves" 

## skipgram


- The skip-gram model considers the conditional probability for generating the context words: “the”, “man”, “his”, and “dog”, which are no more than 2 words away from the center word:

$$
P(\text{the}, \text{man}, \text{his}, \text{dog} \mid \text{loves})
$$


* The skip-gram model assumes the context words are conditionally independent given the center word, so the probability factorizes:

$$
P(\text{the}, \text{man}, \text{his}, \text{dog} \mid \text{loves}) = P(\text{the} \mid \text{loves}) \cdot P(\text{man} \mid \text{loves}) \cdot P(\text{his} \mid \text{loves}) \cdot P(\text{dog} \mid \text{loves})
$$

- Each word in the vocabulary has two $d$-dimensional vector representations (embeddings): 
  - $\mathbf{v}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ when word $i$ is used as a _center_ word  
  - $\mathbf{u}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ when word $i$ is used as a _context_ word  


## Skip-gram model

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Skip-grams** are generalizations of **n-grams** in which we are allowed to skip words, so that the components occur within a specified total number of skipped words.
:::

* An n-gram is a strictly consecutive subsequence of length $n$ of a sequence of tokens $w_1,\ldots, w_m$.
* A $k$-skip-$n$-gram is a length-$n$ subsequence in which a total of at most $k$ words are skipped.
* $k$: the allowance of skipped words (summed over all gaps).
* $n$: the number of words in the extracted subsequence.
* For instance, a $1$-skip $4$-gram is
  - a sequence of 4 words from the text, in order,
  - with at most 1 word skipped in total ($k = 1$).

## Skip-gram model (2) 

* Some $1$-skip $4$-grams of <span style="background-color: #e0f2fe; padding: 2px 6px; border-radius: 4px;">**to be or not to be**</span> are:
  - to be or not: valid (positions 1,2,3,4; 0 words skipped, and $0 \le 1$)
  - to or not to: valid (positions 1,3,4,5; 1 word skipped)
  - be or to be: valid (positions 2,3,5,6; 1 word skipped)
  - to be not be: **not** valid (positions 1,2,4,6; 2 words skipped)


## skip-gram model (3)
 
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
  The training objective of the Skip-gram model is to find word representations that are useful for
predicting the surrounding words in a sentence or a document.
:::

- Given a sequence of training words $w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_T$ and a window size $m$, we maximize the average log probability of the context words:

$$
\max_{\Theta} \; \dfrac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{\substack{-m\leq j\leq m\\ j\neq 0}} \log p(w_{t+j}\mid w_{t})
$$

::: {.small-text}
Here $m$ is the window size: for each center word $w_t$, all context words up to $m$ positions before and after it are used. A larger $m$ gives more training examples and can lead to higher accuracy, at the expense of training time.
:::


## skip-gram model

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
   The basic Skip-gram formulation defines $p(w_{t+j}\mid w_t)$ using the softmax function, which is also often used for 
multiclass predictors in neural networks
:::

![](./img/word-softmax.png){width=70% fig-align="center"}

::: {.small-text}
- softmax turns a collection of numbers into a probability distribution
- $z_i\rightarrow \text{softmax}(z_i)=p_i$ implies that $p_i\geq 0$ (because of the exponentiation) and $\sum p_i=1$ (because of the normalization in the denominator)
:::



## word2vec {#word2vec}

- word2vec  maps each word to a fixed-length vector, and these vectors can better express the similarity and analogy relationship among different words. 

::: {.small-text}
- Mikolov, T. et al. (2013) [Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space. arXiv:1301.3781](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781)
- Mikolov, T. et al. (2013) [Distributed representations of words and phrases and their compositionality. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems. arXiv:1310.4546](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4546)
:::

- word2vec is a classic algorithm that was extremely influential in NLP before the advent of transformer based algorithms.
- The word2vec algorithm has several features that influenced the development of transformers and it is a good place to learn about how embeddings can be created.

::: {.mybox}
**One-hot vectors**:

Before explaining the word2vec algorithm, let's study why semantic vectors are an improvement over one-hot vectors
:::



## One-hot encoding

Sentence: *the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog* (9 tokens, vocabulary size $V = 8$)

| Word | brown | dog | fox | jumps | lazy | over | quick | the |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **the** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | <span style="color:blue">**1**</span> |
| **quick** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | <span style="color:blue">**1**</span> | 0 |
| **brown** | <span style="color:blue">**1**</span> | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **fox** | 0 | 0 | <span style="color:blue">**1**</span> | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **jumps** | 0 | 0 | 0 | <span style="color:blue">**1**</span> | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **over** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | <span style="color:blue">**1**</span> | 0 | 0 |
| **the** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | <span style="color:blue">**1**</span> |
| **lazy** | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | <span style="color:blue">**1**</span> | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| **dog** | 0 | <span style="color:blue">**1**</span> | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

* A <span style="color:blue">one-hot vector</span> is a vector used to represent a categorical value in which exactly one element is 1 and all other elements are 0. Its length equals the vocabulary size $V$.

## Semantics of one-hot vectors

- We would like to be able to test whether, say, "Man" and "Uncle" are relatively similar, but "Tofu" and "Airplane" are not very similar.
- The usual way of comparing vectors^[cosine similarity is defined for non-zero vectors] $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is a cosine similarity (cosine of the angle between the vectors)

$$
\text{cosine similarity}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) =
\dfrac{\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{y}}{\Vert \mathbf{x}\Vert  \Vert \mathbf{y}\Vert }
\in [-1,1]
$$

- cosine similarity between one-hot vectors of any two different words is 0
- One-hot vectors have no natural notion of similarity, e.g., the dot product between the vector for apple and pear would be zero.

## word2vec

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
Word2vec is a group of related models that are used to produce word embeddings, based on a series of extensions of the original Skip-gram model.
:::

* It is mainly  based on two different models: 
  - skip-gram (SG)
  - continuous bag of words (CBOW)^[Continuous bag of words, not covered in this lecture.]
* **word2vec** is a shallow, two-layer neural network trained to reconstruct linguistic contexts of words. 
* **Input**: a large corpus of text 
* **Output**: a vector space, typically of 100-1000 dimensions, with each unique word in the corpus being assigned a corresponding vector in the space. 
* Word vectors are positioned in the vector space such that words that share common contexts in the corpus are located in close proximity to one another in the space.



## distributional similarity

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}

- You shall know a word by the company it keeps J.R. Firth, 1957
- Dime con quién andas, y te diré quién eres (Don Quijote de la Mancha, 1615)
:::
 
* Word2vec essentially looks at the context in which a word appears
* The distribution of a word's neighbors in a large corpus of text approximates the *meaning* of the word

![](./img/quijote.jpg){ fig-align="center"}

## Goal of word2vec
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
  Choose a [dense vector]{.emph} for each word that will be good at predicting which words it co-appears with
:::


 Define a model that predicts the context surrounding a center word $w_t$ using word vectors
$$
\begin{equation}
  p(\text{context}|w_t)=\ldots
\end{equation}
$$

 
* For each position $t=1,\ldots,T$ in the training text, look at the context words within a window of size $m$ around $w_t$. The objective function $J(\Theta)$ is then
$$
J(\Theta)=\prod_{t=1}^{T} \prod_{\substack{-m\le j\le m\\ j\ne 0}} p(w_{t+j}\mid w_t;\Theta)
$$
* We can **simplify** the notation by writing $D$ for the set of all (center, outside) word pairs $(c,o)$ extracted from the text:
$$
J(\Theta)=\prod_{(c,o)\in D} p(o\mid c;\Theta)
$$
* Our goal is to find the parameters $\Theta$ that maximize it: $\hat{\Theta}=\arg\max_{\Theta} J(\Theta)$

## The score: how well do two words fit together?

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
Everything in word2vec is built on one number: the **score** of a (center word, outside word) pair is the dot product of their vectors
:::

$$
s_{o,c}=\mathbf{u}_o^{T}\mathbf{v}_c=\sum_{i=1}^{d} u_{o,i}\,v_{c,i} = \Vert\mathbf{u}_o\Vert\,\Vert\mathbf{v}_c\Vert \cos\theta
$$ {#eq-w2v-score}

* **Large and positive** when the two vectors point in a similar direction: the words tend to occur together
* **Near zero** when the vectors are unrelated (perpendicular)
* **Negative** when they point in opposite directions: the words avoid each other
* This is the cosine similarity from before, without the normalization. Unlike one-hot vectors, whose dot product is always 0 for different words, dense vectors can give graded scores.

## Defining a loss function

* Rather than maximizing the objective function  $J(\Theta)$, it is more convenient to minimize the corresponding loss function

$$
\ell(\Theta)=-\dfrac{1}{|D|} \log J(\Theta)= -\dfrac{1}{|D|} \sum_{(w,c)\in D} \log p(c|w,\Theta)
$$ {#eq-cost}


* We now need to define the term $p(c|w,\Theta)$. We will start off with the **softmax** with $o$: **outside word** and  $c$: **center word** for some skipgram defined by some $t$ and some $j$, i.e., $w_{t+j}$ is shown here as $o$ and $w_t$ is shown as $c$.

$$
 p(w_{t+j}|w_t,\Theta) =  p(o|c) = \dfrac{\exp (\mathbf{u}_{o}^{T}\mathbf{v}_c) }{\sum_{w=1}^{V} \exp (\mathbf{u}_{w}^{T}\mathbf{v}_c)}
$$ {#eq-loss-per-word}
 
::: {.small-text}
* $V$: the total number of vocabulary of words 
* $T$: the total number of words in a large corpus (where individual words are repeated).
:::
 
## Two vectors per word
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
Each word actually has two vector representations, both in $\mathbb{R}^d$
:::

* $\mathbf{v}_c$ is the representation of a word when it is the center word of the window
* $\mathbf{u}_o$ is the representation of a word when it is an outside (context) word of the center word
* In this model the position of the context word in the window is not important: the same softmax is used for every offset $j$
* After training, the vectors $\mathbf{v}$ (or the average of $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$) are used as the word embeddings
 
 
## word2vec: from one-hot vector to embedding
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
The first layer is a lookup: multiplying the one-hot vector of the center word by the matrix $\mathbf{W}$ selects that word's vector.
:::

Let $\mathbf{x}_c \in \{0,1\}^{V}$ be the one-hot vector of the center word $c$ and let $\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times V}$ be a randomly initialized matrix whose columns are the center-word vectors. Then

$$
\mathbf{v}_c = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}_c
$$

$$
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}
  \ldots & \ldots & 0.2 & \ldots & \ldots \\
  \ldots & \ldots & -1.4 & \ldots & \ldots \\
  \ldots & \ldots & 0.3 & \ldots & \ldots \\
  && \vdots && \\
  \ldots & \ldots & 0.7 & \ldots & \ldots \\
  \ldots & \ldots & 0.6 & \ldots & \ldots
\end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{W}\;(d\times V)}
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0\\ 0\\ 1\\ 0\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{x}_c\;(V\times 1)}
=
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0.2\\ -1.4\\ 0.3\\ \vdots \\ 0.7 \\ 0.6 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{v}_c\;(d\times 1)}
$$

## word2vec: calculate the loss

::: {.small-text}
We have a second matrix $\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d}$ whose *rows* are the outside-word vectors $\mathbf{u}_w^{T}$ (whereas the *columns* of $\mathbf{W}$ are the center-word vectors).
Multiplying by $\mathbf{v}_c$ gives one score for every word in the vocabulary:
:::

$$
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}
  \mathbf{u}_1^{T} \\ \mathbf{u}_2^{T} \\ \mathbf{u}_3^{T} \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{u}_{V}^{T}
\end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{U}\;(V\times d)}
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0.2\\ -1.4\\ 0.3\\ \vdots \\ 0.7 \\ 0.6 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{v}_c\;(d\times 1)}
=
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}
  \mathbf{u}_1^{T}\mathbf{v}_c \\ \mathbf{u}_2^{T}\mathbf{v}_c \\ \mathbf{u}_3^{T}\mathbf{v}_c \\ \vdots \\ \mathbf{u}_{V}^{T}\mathbf{v}_c
\end{bmatrix}}_{\text{scores}\;(V\times 1)}
$$

## word2vec: calculate the loss (2)

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
To calculate the loss, we apply the softmax to the scores $\mathbf{U}\mathbf{v}_c$ and compare the result to the *truth* vector $\mathbf{y}$, a one-hot vector that marks the word that really occurred in the context.
:::

$$
\text{softmax}(\mathbf{U}\mathbf{v}_c) =
\begin{bmatrix} p_1\\ p_2\\ p_3\\ \vdots \\ p_{V-1} \\ p_{V} \end{bmatrix},
\qquad p_w = p(w \mid c)
$$

If the truth vector has a one at position $o$, the loss for this example is $-\log p_o$ (the cross-entropy between $\mathbf{y}$ and the predicted distribution). It is small when the model gives the true outside word a probability near 1.


## word2vec: the parameters
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
As is usual in deep learning, we will train the model using gradient descent. We first collect all of the parameters, i.e., both the center vectors ($\mathbf{v}$) and the outside vectors ($\mathbf{u}$) of all words, in a single vector $\Theta$.
:::

$$
\Theta = \begin{bmatrix}
           \mathbf{v}_{aardvark} \\ \vdots \\  \mathbf{v}_{zebra} \\  \mathbf{u}_{aardvark} \\ \vdots \\  \mathbf{u}_{zebra}
          \end{bmatrix}
\in \mathbb{R}^{2dV}
$$

::: {.small-text}
There is a $d$-dimensional vector for each of the $V$ words, and each word is represented twice (as center and as outside word). All of this is flattened into a $2dV \times 1$ vector $\Theta$, which contains the columns of $\mathbf{W}$ and the rows of $\mathbf{U}$.
For example, with $V=100{,}000$ and $d=300$ there are $60$ million parameters.
:::


## gradient descent
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
We use gradient descent^[Refer to previous two lectures for details] to find the vectors that minimize the loss.
:::

* For a single (center, outside) pair $(c,o)$ we need the gradient of $\log p(o\mid c)$. 
* The loss is $-\log p(o\mid c)$, so its gradient is the negative of this.
* We compute it with respect to the center vector $\mathbf{v}_c$; the gradient with respect to the outside vectors $\mathbf{u}_w$ is similar.

$$
\begin{eqnarray*}
\log p(w_{t+j}\mid w_t) &=& \log p(o\mid c) \\
&=& \log \dfrac{\exp (\mathbf{u}_{o}^{T}\mathbf{v}_{c})}{\sum_{w=1}^{V} \exp (\mathbf{u}_{w}^{T}\mathbf{v}_{c})} \\
&=& \mathbf{u}_{o}^{T}\mathbf{v}_{c} - \log \sum_{w=1}^{V} \exp (\mathbf{u}_{w}^{T}\mathbf{v}_{c})
\end{eqnarray*}
$$

We will differentiate the two terms separately.
 
## gradient descent

- For the first term we have:
$$
\nabla_{\mathbf{v}_c}\, \mathbf{u}_{o}^{T}\mathbf{v}_{c} = \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{v}_{c}} \mathbf{u}_{o}^{T}\mathbf{v}_{c} = \mathbf{u}_{o}
$$

- For the second term, recall the chain rule $\frac{d}{dx} f(g(x)) = f^{\prime}(g(x))\cdot g^{\prime}(x)$. 
- Here $f=\log$ is the outer function, $g(\mathbf{v}_c)=\sum_{w=1}^{V} \exp(\mathbf{u}_w^{T}\mathbf{v}_c)$ is the inner function, and $\frac{d}{dx}\log x = \frac{1}{x}$. 
- We use $x$ as the summation index of the inner sum, to avoid confusion with the $w$ in the denominator.


$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{v}_{c}}  \log \sum_{w=1}^{V} \exp(\mathbf{u}_w^{T}\mathbf{v}_c) =
\dfrac{1}{\sum_{w=1}^{V} \exp(\mathbf{u}_w^{T}\mathbf{v}_c)}  \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{v}_{c}}  \sum_{x=1}^{V} \exp(\mathbf{u}_x^{T}\mathbf{v}_c)
$$

::: {.tiny-credit}
Note that in this equation, $\log$ plays the role of the outer function $f$ and 
$\sum_{w=1}^{V} \exp(\mathbf{u}_w^{T}\mathbf{v}_c)$ is the inner function $g$; 
the first derivative of $\log x$ is $\dfrac{1}{x}$.
:::

## gradient descent (3)

We still need the derivative of the sum from the previous slide:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{v}_{c}} \sum_{x=1}^{V} \exp(\mathbf{u}_x^{T}\mathbf{v}_c)
 &= \sum_{x=1}^{V}\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{v}_{c}} \exp(\mathbf{u}_x^{T}\mathbf{v}_c) \\
 &= \sum_{x=1}^{V} \exp(\mathbf{u}_x^{T}\mathbf{v}_c) \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{v}_{c}} \mathbf{u}_x^{T}\mathbf{v}_c \\
 &= \sum_{x=1}^{V} \exp(\mathbf{u}_x^{T}\mathbf{v}_c)\, \mathbf{u}_x
\end{aligned}
$$

* The first line holds because the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives.
* The second line follows from the chain rule and the fact that $\frac{d e^x}{dx}=e^x$.

## gradient descent (4)

Pulling the parts together:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{v}_{c}}  \log \dfrac{\exp (\mathbf{u}_{o}^{T}\mathbf{v}_{c})}{\sum_{w=1}^{V} \exp (\mathbf{u}_{w}^{T}\mathbf{v}_{c})}
&= \mathbf{u}_{o}  - \dfrac{1}{\sum_{w=1}^{V} \exp(\mathbf{u}_w^{T}\mathbf{v}_c)}  \sum_{x=1}^{V}  \exp(\mathbf{u}_x^{T}\mathbf{v}_c)\,\mathbf{u}_x \\
&= \mathbf{u}_{o}  -  \sum_{x=1}^{V} \dfrac{\exp(\mathbf{u}_x^{T}\mathbf{v}_c)}{\sum_{w=1}^{V} \exp(\mathbf{u}_w^{T}\mathbf{v}_c)}\,\mathbf{u}_x
\end{aligned}
$$


The second line holds because $\dfrac{1}{\sum_{w=1}^{V} \exp(\mathbf{u}_w^{T}\mathbf{v}_c)}$ is just a scalar and can be pulled into the sum.

The fraction inside the sum is exactly the <span style="color:blue">softmax</span> probability that word $x$ occurs as an outside word of the center word $c$:

$$
p(x\mid c)=\dfrac{\exp(\mathbf{u}_x^{T}\mathbf{v}_c)}{\sum_{w=1}^{V} \exp(\mathbf{u}_w^{T}\mathbf{v}_c)}
$$
 
## gradient descent (5)
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
Therefore, the gradient actually has the form of an observed value ($\mathbf{u}_o$) subtracted by the expectation across all context words 
:::

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \mathbf{v}_{c}} \log p(o\mid c) = \mathbf{u}_{o} -  \sum_{x=1}^{V} p(x\mid c)\,\mathbf{u}_x
$$

* The probabilities $p(\cdot\mid c)=\text{softmax}(\mathbf{U}\mathbf{v}_c)$ form a vector of length $V$. In matrix form the gradient is $\mathbf{U}^{T}(\mathbf{y}-p(\cdot\mid c))$, where $\mathbf{y}$ is the one-hot truth vector.
* $\Theta$ has $2Vd$ entries, but for one training pair the gradient is nonzero only for $\mathbf{v}_c$ and the outside vectors $\mathbf{u}_w$.


## gradient descent (6)
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
To minimize the loss $\ell(\Theta)$ we take a step against its gradient with learning rate $\eta$. For a single training pair $(c,o)$ (stochastic gradient descent) the update for the center vector is
:::

$$
\mathbf{v}_c \;\gets\; \mathbf{v}_c + \eta \left[ \mathbf{u}_{o} -  \sum_{x=1}^{V} p(x\mid c)\,\mathbf{u}_x \right]
$$

The plus sign appears because the loss is $-\log p(o\mid c)$, so its gradient is the negative of the bracket.

- $\eta$ is the learning rate
- $+\eta\,\mathbf{u}_o$ moves $\mathbf{v}_c$ towards the vector $\mathbf{u}_o$ of the word that actually occurred in the context
- $-\eta\,\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p(\cdot\mid c)}[\mathbf{u}_x]$ moves $\mathbf{v}_c$ away from the expected outside vector
- The expectation is taken over every word $x\in V$ in the vocabulary, using the model's own distribution $p(x\mid c)$ (the softmax output)
- The exact gradient is [expensive]{.emph}: the expectation touches every word vector in the vocabulary at every training step. 
- This is the practical bottleneck that motivates approximations like [negative sampling]{.emph}, which replaces the full sum with a small sample of "negative" words




## word2vec: scaling up
![](./img/softmax-classifier.png){width=40% fig-align="center"}

* The softmax is very expensive: to compute and normalize one probability we need the score of **every** one of the $V$ words in the vocabulary, at every training step.

## word2vec: scaling up
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
  word2vec therefore is trained to discriminate the real target words $w_t$ from $k$ imaginary (noise) words $\tilde{w}$, in the same context.
:::

![](./img/noise-classifier.png){width=40% fig-align="center"}

## Negative sampling {#negsample}

- Consider a pair $(c,o)$ of a center word and an outside word
- The probability that this pair came from the corpus is $p(Z=1\mid c,o;\Theta)$ (i.e., it corresponded to a skip-gram in the actual data)
- The probability that the pair did not come from the corpus is $p(Z=0\mid c,o;\Theta) = 1 - p(Z=1\mid c,o;\Theta)$

* **Goal**: find parameters $\Theta$ that maximize the probability that all of the observed pairs indeed come from the data

$$
\begin{align*}
& \arg \max_{\Theta} \prod_{(c,o)\in D} p(Z=1\mid c,o;\Theta)\\
&=\arg \max_{\Theta} \log \prod_{(c,o)\in D} p(Z=1\mid c,o;\Theta)\\
&=\arg \max_{\Theta}  \sum_{(c,o)\in D} \log p(Z=1\mid c,o;\Theta)
\end{align*}
$$

* On its own this objective has a trivial solution (make every pair look real), which is why negative examples are needed


## Negative sampling (2)

- The probability $p(Z=1\mid c,o;\Theta)$ can be defined using the sigmoid function $\sigma(x) = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}$ applied to the same score as before:
- Recall $\mathbf{u}_o^{T}\mathbf{v}_c$ (c.f. @eq-w2v-score), the score of each pair of words
$$
p(Z=1\mid c,o;\Theta) = \sigma(\mathbf{u}_o^{T}\mathbf{v}_c) = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-\mathbf{u}_o^{T}\mathbf{v}_c}}
$$

We can now rewrite the objective function:

$$
\arg \max_{\Theta}  \sum_{(c,o)\in D} \log \sigma(\mathbf{u}_o^{T}\mathbf{v}_c)
$$

## Negative sampling (3): adding negative examples

- Maximizing only $\sum_{D}\log\sigma(\mathbf{u}_o^{T}\mathbf{v}_c)$ is not enough: it can be made large by making all scores large. We therefore add **negative examples**: a set $D^{\prime}$ of pairs $(c,\tilde{o})$ that did *not* come from the corpus. Each is made by pairing a center word with a randomly drawn word, which is presumed to be unrelated to it.
- We now maximize the probability that real pairs are labelled $Z=1$ and noise pairs are labelled $Z=0$:

$$
\begin{align*}
&\arg\max_{\Theta} \prod_{(c,o)\in D}p(Z=1\mid c,o;\Theta)
 \prod_{(c,\tilde{o})\in D^{\prime}}p(Z=0\mid c,\tilde{o};\Theta) \\
&= \arg\max_{\Theta} \sum_{(c,o)\in D}\log p(Z=1\mid c,o;\Theta)
 + \sum_{(c,\tilde{o})\in D^{\prime}} \log \bigl(1- p(Z=1\mid c,\tilde{o};\Theta)\bigr) \\
&= \arg\max_{\Theta} \sum_{(c,o)\in D}\log \sigma(\mathbf{u}_o^{T}\mathbf{v}_c)
 + \sum_{(c,\tilde{o})\in D^{\prime}} \log \sigma(-\mathbf{u}_{\tilde{o}}^{T}\mathbf{v}_c)
\end{align*}
$$

::: {.small-text}
* The second line takes the logarithm (the maximizer does not change, and the product becomes a sum). 
* The third line uses $p(Z=1\mid\cdot)=\sigma(\mathbf{u}^{T}\mathbf{v}_c)$ and the identity $1-\sigma(x)=\sigma(-x)$.^[See [lecture 4](./logreg.qmd)]
:::

## Negative sampling (4): choosing the negatives

- $D^{\prime}$ could contain every wrong word for every center word, up to $V-1$ pairs per positive pair, which would bring back the cost of the full softmax. Instead we **sample** the negatives.
- For each $(c,o)\in D$ we draw $k$ random words $\tilde{o}_1,\ldots,\tilde{o}_k$ and use the pairs $(c,\tilde{o}_1),\ldots,(c,\tilde{o}_k)$ as presumed negatives. So there are $k$ times as many negative as positive examples.
- The unigram distribution is the relative frequency of each word in the training corpus. Words $\tilde{o}_j$ are drawn from the unigram distribution **raised to the power 3/4** and renormalized:

$$
P_{n}(w)=
\frac{\mathrm{count}(w)^{3/4}}
{\sum_{w^{\prime}} \mathrm{count}(w^{\prime})^{3/4}}
$$

- This downweights frequent words and upweights rare ones. For example, relative frequencies $0.90,\ 0.09,\ 0.01$ become about $0.83,\ 0.15,\ 0.03$.

::: {.tiny-credit}
Mikolov T, Sutskever I, Chen K, Corrado GS, Dean J (2013) [Distributed representations of words and phrases and their compositionality. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 26](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/2999792.2999959).
:::



## Concept replacement {#concept}

The original word2vec method operates on individual words (tokens). However, many medical concepts span multiple tokens. For instance, <span style="background-color: #e0f2fe; padding: 2px 6px; border-radius: 4px;">non-small-cell lung carcinoma</span> would be treated by word2vec as three or five tokens (depending on how the hyphen is handled in preprocessing), but it represents a single medical concept.

- Some approaches collapse multiword concepts into a single token before embedding, by replacing each mention with a **concept ID**. For instance, <span style="background-color: #e0f2fe; padding: 2px 6px; border-radius: 4px;">non-small-cell lung carcinoma</span> can be replaced by its MeSH ID D002289.
- Synonyms ("NSCLC", "non small cell lung cancer", ...) are replaced by the same ID and therefore share one embedding.
- This requires concept recognition: finding the mentions in the text and linking them to the correct ID, a step that has errors of its own.

## Tokens {#token}
::: {.callout-important icon="true" appearance="default" title="The need for tokenization"}

* LLMs (and many other machine learning algorithms) process numbers rather than text
* Therefore, text must first be converted to numbers.
:::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

Tokenization by OpenAI

![Created with <https://platform.openai.com/tokenizer>](img/tokenizing.png){width=80% fig-align="center"}

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

* A __token__ is an entry in the tokenizer's fixed __vocabulary__ (a word, a part of a word, or a single character). Each token has an integer, its __token ID__ (or __token index__).
* Here we see an example GPT subword tokenization of the word *discombobulate*:
    - dis: 4220
    - comb: 43606
    - ob: 630
    - ulate: 10111
* The IDs are arbitrary labels: the fact that 4220 is close to 4221 means nothing.^[See [tiktokenizer](https://tiktokenizer.vercel.app/) for an app to visualize different tokenizing schemes.]

:::
:::

## Tokenization (2)

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition
**Tokenization** is the process of converting a sequence of text into smaller parts, known as tokens. Tokens can be as small as single characters or as long as words.
:::

::: {.token-table}

| Method | Granularity | Example | Pros | Cons |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **Word** | Full words | ["machine", "learning"] | High semantic clarity | Massive vocabulary; fails on unknown words |
| **Subword** | Meaningful chunks | ["machine", "learn", "ing"] | Handles new words well | Vocabulary must be learned from data (e.g., BPE); longer sequences than words |
| **Character** | Individual letters | ["m", "a", "c", "h", "i", "n", "e", "␣", "l", "e", "a", "r", "n", "i", "n", "g"] | Tiny vocabulary; no unknown words | Loses semantic meaning; very long sequences |

:::


## Words, characters, and subwords

**Problems with word-level vocabularies**

- There are extremely many unique words in natural language
- Words have different lexical forms (run, runs, ran, running, ...)
- Out-of-vocabulary words cannot be represented

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.hl-container}
![](img/char-embed.png){width="100%"}
:::

::: {.tiny-credit}
Embeddings of characters, projected to 2D: digits, uppercase, lowercase and punctuation each form a cluster. Image credit: <https://github.com/minimaxir/char-embeddings>
:::
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}

**Limitations of character-level models**

  - Sequences become very long, which makes training and inference expensive
  - A single character carries almost no meaning
  - Unicode has more than 150K characters

**Subword tokens**: a vocabulary of tens of thousands of pieces, no out-of-vocabulary words, and much shorter sequences than characters.

:::
:::


## Tokens are then converted to embeddings

- LLMs do not use tokens directly, but instead convert input tokens to embeddings
- Embeddings are dense numeric representations of tokens
- During training, an LLM [learns]{.emph} embeddings to represent individual tokens

```{python}
#| label: fig-token-embeddings
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Tokenization and embedding (illustrative vectors; the first 3 of $d$ dimensions are shown)"
token_embeddings()
```

## Byte Pair Encoding {#bytepair}

- Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) is a simple, greedy algorithm. It starts from single characters (or bytes) and repeatedly **merges the most frequent pair of adjacent symbols** into one new symbol.
- Each merge shortens the text and adds one entry to the vocabulary. The list of merges, in order, is stored as a table of **merge rules**.
- The merge rules are all we need to tokenize new text: apply them in the same order to its characters.
- Originally a compression algorithm ([Gage, 1994](https://jacobfilipp.com/DrDobbs/articles/CUJ/1994/9402/gage/gage.htm))
- adapted for subword tokenization in NLP by [Sennrich et al. (2016)](https://aclanthology.org/P16-1162/).


## BPE: a small example

- BPE is widely used in the preprocessing stage of training large language models
- Two different merge sequences for the input $s= \mathrm{aabaaaba}$:

$$
\begin{alignat}{3}
\mathrm{aabaaaba} &\to \mathrm{XbXaba} &&\to \mathrm{YXaba} &&\to \mathrm{Zaba} \\
\mathrm{aabaaaba} &\to \mathrm{aXaaXa} &&\to \phantom{\mathrm{Y}}\mathrm{YaYa} &&\to \mathrm{ZZ}
\end{alignat}
$$

- Top: merges $\mathrm{aa} \to \mathrm{X}$, $\mathrm{Xb} \to \mathrm{Y}$, $\mathrm{YX}\to \mathrm{Z}$
- Bottom: merges $\mathrm{ab} \to \mathrm{X}$, $\mathrm{aX} \to \mathrm{Y}$, $\mathrm{Ya}\to \mathrm{Z}$
- The *utility* of a merge sequence is the number of symbols saved, $|s|-|s^{\prime}|$:
  - top: $8-4=4$; bottom: $8-2=6$
- In the first step, $\mathrm{aa}$, $\mathrm{ab}$ and $\mathrm{ba}$ can each be replaced twice, so a greedy algorithm may pick any of them. The choice changes the final result: greedy merging is not guaranteed to be optimal.

## Problem definition (1)

- Consider an input string $s$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$ of symbols (merging will add new symbols to the alphabet)
- Write the concatenation of strings $a$ and $b$ as $a\cdot b$ (sometimes simply $ab$ when clear from context)
- The length of a string $a$ is $|a|$, its $i^{th}$ character is $a[i]$, and the substring $a[i]\cdot a[i+1]\cdots a[j]$ (both end points included) is $a[i:j]$
- A **replacement rule** $\mathrm{replace}_{x\to y}$ transforms a string $s$ by replacing the occurrences of the string $x$ in $s$ with the string $y$, scanning from left to right without overlaps:
  - If $s$ does not contain $x$, then $\mathrm{replace}_{x\to y}(s) = s$
  - Otherwise, let $i\ge 0$ be the number of symbols before the first occurrence of $x$, i.e., the smallest $i$ with $s[i+1 : i+|x|] = x$. Then

$$
\mathrm{replace}_{x\to y}(s) = s[1:i]\cdot y\cdot \mathrm{replace}_{x\to y}\bigl(s[i+|x|+1:|s|]\bigr)
$$

- Example: $\mathrm{replace}_{\mathrm{aa}\to\mathrm{X}}(\mathrm{aabaaaba}) = \mathrm{XbXaba}$ (in $\mathrm{aaa}$ only the leftmost $\mathrm{aa}$ is replaced)

## Problem definition (2)

- A sequence of replacement rules $\mathbb{R} = (\mathbb{R}_1,\ldots ,\mathbb{R}_k)$ with $\mathbb{R}_i = \mathrm{replace}_{a_ib_i\to c_i}$, where $a_i$, $b_i$ and $c_i$ are symbols, is called a **merge sequence** of length $k$.
- Applying it to $s$ means applying $\mathbb{R}_1$ first, then $\mathbb{R}_2$, and so on: $s^{\prime} =(\mathbb{R}_k \circ \cdots \circ \mathbb{R}_1)(s)$, where $\circ$ is function composition.
- $|s^{\prime}|$ is the **compressed length**, and $|s| - |s^{\prime}|$ is the **utility** of $\mathbb{R}$ for $s$.

- BPE starts from the input string $s$ and performs $k$ merge steps. In each step it replaces *all* occurrences of one pair, choosing the pair whose replacement gives the largest utility (the pair with the most non-overlapping occurrences).
- How many symbols does the vocabulary contain after $k$ merges?

. . .

- $|\Sigma|+k$: each merge adds exactly one new symbol $c_i$. (GPT-2: 256 bytes + 50,000 merges + 1 end-of-text token = 50,257.)

## BPE algorithm

**Input:** a text corpus $s$ and the number of merges $k$ (the final vocabulary has $|\Sigma|+k$ symbols)

- Let $s^{(0)} = s$
- For $i = 1,\ldots,k$:
  1. Choose the pair of symbols $a_ib_i$ for which replacing it gives the shortest string $s^{(i)}=\mathbb{R}_i(s^{(i-1)})$. Break ties by a fixed rule (e.g., the lexicographically smallest pair).
  2. Create a new symbol $c_i$ that is not in $\Sigma$ and differs from $c_1,\ldots,c_{i-1}$.
  3. Let $\mathbb{R}_i = \mathrm{replace}_{a_ib_i\to c_i}$ and apply it.
- **Output:** the merge sequence $\mathbb{R} = (\mathbb{R}_1,\ldots ,\mathbb{R}_k)$

[HOMEWORK]{.hw-badge} You will implement a version of BPE


## BPE Applications

::: {.mybox}
**LLMs and BPE**

Most major LLMs use BPE, or a close variant, to transform input text into sequences of integers (token IDs), which the model then maps to embeddings

- GPT models (byte-level BPE, introduced with GPT-2)
- Llama
- Mistral
:::

::: {.small-text}
Not all do: BERT uses WordPiece, and T5 uses a unigram language-model tokenizer.
:::

## BPE Applications (2)

- BPE balances between character-level (long sequences, so slow) and word-level (too many parameters for rare words, poor generalization)
- BPE handles rare words (e.g., those not in the training vocabulary) by falling back to smaller subwords or individual characters/bytes
- Frequent affixes ("ing", "ed", "tion", "pre", "un") tend to become tokens of their own, so the model can share information between word forms. The merges are statistical, not linguistic, so they do not always match morphemes
- Cross-lingual: shared pieces can relate cognates in different languages (Produktion, production, producción, ...).



## BPE Applications (3)

- Better parameter efficiency: Model spends capacity on meaningful patterns rather than memorizing every word variant.
- Consider the German word "Abwasserbehandlungsanlage"
  - If a model created a single token for this word, it would need to learn the meaning of the token from relatively rare mentions in the training data
  - If the model splits this into "Abwasser", "Behandlung(s)" and "Anlage", the meanings of these three tokens are inferred from a much richer context in the training data 
- Consider word families:
  - "happy": happy, happier, happiest, happily, happiness, unhappy, unhappier, unhappiest, unhappily, unhappiness
  - "nation": nations, national, nationally, nationalist, nationalists, nationalism, nationalistic, nationality, nationalities, nationalize, nationalized, nationalization, international, internationally, transnational, multinational.
- BPE often will extract a common root from families such as this -- the model learns one embedding for the shared root and separate embeddings for the inflectional/derivational endings

:::{.tiny-credit}
Sennrich, R, et al. (2016) [Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units](https://aclanthology.org/P16-1162/)
:::

## Strawberry

::: {.mybox}
**Older versions of GPT** famously were not able to determine how many r's there are in the word strawberry
:::

![](./img/strawberry.png){width=40% fig-align="center"}

- Why do you think this is?

## Strawberry tokens

<span style="background-color: #e0f2fe; padding: 2px 6px; border-radius: 4px; font-family: monospace; font-size: 1.4em;">str</span>
<span style="background-color: #fef3c7; padding: 2px 6px; border-radius: 4px; font-family: monospace; font-size: 1.4em;">aw</span>
<span style="background-color: #dcfce7; padding: 2px 6px; border-radius: 4px; font-family: monospace; font-size: 1.4em;">berry</span>

::: {.small-text}
Example tokenization from the OpenAI tokenizer
:::

- The model does not see letters: it sees three token IDs. The r's are hidden inside the tokens (1 in *str*, 0 in *aw*, 2 in *berry*)
- BPE merges frequent character sequences into single tokens, which hides the letters inside them
- LLMs work with embedding vectors derived from tokens. Sometimes those tokens and their embeddings correspond to our conceptualization of language, and sometimes they do not
- Newer LLMs often get this right, e.g., by spelling the word out letter by letter first, or by running a small script to count
